html_075: To Kill a Mockingbird · Book Info
js_003: Who is the American novelist who wrote To Kill a Mockingbird?
js_005: John Steinbeck, who wrote The Grapes of Wrath
js_006: Margaret Mitchell, of Gone with the Wind
js_007: William Faulkner, who wrote The Sound and the Fury
js_008: To Kill a Mockingbird is the debut novel of Alabama-born writer Harper Lee (1926–2016), published in 1960. For decades she was known as the author of just this one book, and it made her an icon of American literature.
js_010: Which year was this novel first published in the US?
js_012: 1945, the year World War II ended
js_013: 2016, the year the author passed away
js_015: It was first published on July 11, 1960 by the American publisher J. B. Lippincott & Co. It won the Pulitzer the following year and has since sold over 30 million copies worldwide as an enduring classic.
js_017: Who narrates this story from childhood memory?
js_020: Dill, the friend who visits every summer
js_021: Her father, the lawyer Atticus Finch
js_022: The story unfolds in the voice of six-year-old Scout (Jean Louise Finch). The overlap between a child’s eyes and the adult she later becomes is one of the novel’s great charms.
js_024: What is the job of Scout’s father, Atticus Finch?
js_029: Atticus works as a lawyer in Maycomb and has also served in the state legislature. He’s portrayed as a father who teaches his children through his own actions rather than lectures.
js_031: What is the small, fictional Southern town where the story takes place?
js_032: Maycomb, a small town in Alabama
js_036: The setting is Maycomb, a fictional town in Alabama. In this small, close-knit town during the height of the Depression in the 1930s, everyone knows everyone — and that world is the entire universe of the novel.
js_037: What is the name of Scout’s brother, four years older than her?
js_042: Her brother Jem (Jeremy Atticus Finch) is at Scout’s side throughout the story. He’s also the character most shaken — and most transformed — by the trial.
js_043: Who is the boy who comes to stay with his aunt every summer and hangs out with the Finch siblings?
js_048: Dill (Charles Baker Harris) is the summer visitor and mastermind of every adventure. The game of trying to lure the recluse out of his house is his idea.
js_049: Who is the neighbor who hasn’t left his house in decades and has become the subject of the children’s rumors?
js_050: Arthur Radley, whom the kids call Boo
js_054: Boo Radley (Arthur Radley) is a recluse almost no one has ever seen. The children imagine him as a monster, but the novel shows just how wrong that imagination turns out to be.
js_056: What is the name of the young Black man Atticus takes on as a client?
js_058: Reverend Sykes, of the Black church
js_059: Judge John Taylor, who presides over the trial
js_061: Tom Robinson is charged with raping a white woman. Once Atticus agrees to defend him, the Finch family becomes the target of the town’s scorn.
js_062: Who is the Black housekeeper who runs the Finch household and essentially helps raise the children?
js_067: Calpurnia is strict yet warm — essentially a mother figure. She takes the children to her Black church, showing them the other half of Maycomb.
js_080: Harper Lee’s full name was Nelle Harper Lee. She grew up in Monroeville, Alabama, the daughter of a lawyer — and that town and her father became the models for Maycomb and Atticus.
js_081: The book was a sensation from its first year and won the Pulitzer the next. It’s been translated into more than 40 languages and became a staple of American school reading lists.
js_082: Scout hates dresses and leads with her fists. As the story goes on, she learns to stand in someone else’s shoes instead of swinging at them.
js_083: Atticus has been named the greatest hero in 100 years of American film. But that image cracked in 2015 with the publication of Go Set a Watchman.
js_084: The real-life model for Maycomb is Monroeville, Alabama, where the author grew up. Even today, the old courthouse there stages the novel every year.
js_085: Jem can’t accept the verdict and falls apart. It’s the growing pain of a child realizing, for the first time, that the adult world isn’t fair.
js_086: Dill’s real-life model, Truman Capote, went on to write In Cold Blood. The two were childhood best friends who lived next door to each other.
js_087: Boo Radley doesn’t show himself until almost the very end of the novel. His presence grows only through rumor — until he finally appears wearing an entirely different face.
js_088: Tom Robinson is a hardworking man and father of three. The simple fact that he helped Mayella is used against him in court.
js_089: Calpurnia speaks two languages — proper English at the Finch house, and the speech of her neighbors at her Black church. It’s the first time Scout is truly startled by this.
js_102: ↻ This question will come back later
js_104: A bird that does no harm and only sings. This novel’s core symbol, standing for both Tom Robinson and Boo Radley.
js_106: Atticus’s lesson that you can’t truly know someone until you’ve stood in their shoes. It’s the key that unlocks the whole novel.
js_108: The evidence falls apart, but the verdict is guilty. It shows what happens when a courtroom judges by skin color instead of truth.
js_110: The monster that rumor built. In reality, just a neighbor who left gifts in a tree hollow and quietly watched over the kids.
js_112: Starting something you know you’ll lose, and seeing it through anyway. This is Atticus’s definition of real courage.
js_114: 1930s Alabama, where segregation and discrimination were the law. The backdrop against which the trial’s outcome was already decided.
js_116: A real case in which Black teenagers were wrongfully charged. It gave the novel’s courtroom scenes the true air of their era.
js_118: A beloved classic that draws just as much criticism. Ongoing debate centers on Black characters staying in the background, and on repeated attempts to ban the book.
js_120: A Maycomb Summer — The House of Rumors
js_121: The story opens in Depression-era Maycomb, Alabama, a town where everyone knows everyone.
js_122: The Radley house, where Boo hasn’t come out in decades, becomes the children’s biggest fascination.
js_123: When Dill arrives for the summer, the game of luring the recluse outside begins.
js_124: At school, Scout gets scolded by her teacher for not understanding the Cunningham boy’s situation.
js_125: Gum and coins turn up in a hollow in the Radleys’ fence tree.
js_127: The Tree Hollow and the Blanket — An Unseen Hand
js_128: Miss Maudie calmly tells the children about the Radley family’s history.
js_129: Sneaking over the fence at night, Jem loses his pants and later finds them mended and hanging in place.
js_130: The gifts in the hollow grow more thoughtful — even a soap carving and a pocket watch appear.
js_131: Boo’s brother Nathan seals the hollow with cement, cutting off the silent conversation.
js_132: On a freezing night during a neighbor’s house fire, someone drapes a blanket over Scout’s shoulders.
js_134: A Father’s Choice — The Mad Dog and the Camellias
js_135: The town turns its back once Atticus takes on Tom Robinson’s defense.
js_136: When someone insults her father, Scout throws a punch — and Atticus tells her to hold back.
js_137: Atticus reveals a hidden skill, dropping a rabid dog, Tim Johnson, with a single shot.
js_138: Worn down by cruel remarks, Jem destroys every camellia in Mrs. Dubose’s yard.
js_139: The reading sessions given as punishment turn out to be part of her fight to break a morphine addiction before she dies.
js_141: Two Maycombs — Church and the Jailhouse
js_142: Calpurnia takes the children to her Black church, revealing the town’s other half.
js_143: Aunt Alexandra arrives, determined to uphold the Finch family’s reputation.
js_144: Dill, unable to go home, is found hiding under Scout’s bed.
js_145: Atticus stands guard alone outside the jailhouse, and a mob gathers at night.
js_146: When Scout speaks up to Mr. Cunningham, the crowd quietly disperses.
js_148: Three Days in Court — Evidence and Verdict
js_149: With the whole town packed into the courtroom, the children watch the trial from the balcony reserved for Black spectators.
js_150: Atticus has Bob Ewell write his name, revealing that he’s left-handed.
js_151: The court confirms that Tom’s left arm has been useless since an accident.
js_152: One line — that Tom felt sorry for Mayella — seals his fate.
js_153: The verdict comes back guilty, and everyone in the Black section rises to their feet.
js_155: After the Verdict — Halloween Night and the Porch
js_156: Jem falls apart, realizing for the first time that the adult world isn’t fair.
js_157: Word arrives that Tom was shot dead trying to climb a prison fence.
js_158: At the Halloween pageant, Scout heads home in a giant ham costume.
js_159: In the dark, Bob Ewell attacks the siblings — until someone appears and saves them.
js_160: Standing on the Radley porch, Scout looks down the street through her neighbor’s eyes.
js_161: A Word of Greeting Outside the Jailhouse
js_162: Facing a mob that’s come to drag Tom out, Scout — unaware of what’s happening — strikes up small talk with Mr. Walter Cunningham about his son. Called by name, he steps out of the anonymous crowd and becomes an individual again, and the mob quietly disperses.
js_163: Crowds turn fiercest when they’re faceless. This scene shows the power in simply calling someone by name.
js_165: Worn down by cruel words, Jem destroys every camellia bush belonging to the elderly neighbor. The weeks of reading aloud as punishment turn out to have been one woman’s last fight to kick a morphine habit before she died.
js_166: Atticus called her the bravest person he ever knew. How often do we recognize someone who starts a fight they know they can’t win?
js_167: The Truth the Sheriff Covered Up
js_168: On the night Bob Ewell dies, Sheriff Heck Tate decides to say he fell on his own knife. It was to keep the man who saved the children out of the public eye.
js_169: A decision that breaks the law but sides with conscience. When rules and justice pull in different directions, what should we go by?
js_170: Whose shoes have I actually stood in lately?
js_171: Atticus said you can’t really know someone until you climb into their skin and walk around in it. Think of one person you’ve found hardest to understand lately.
js_172: Is there something I need to start, even knowing I might lose?
js_173: Atticus taught that sometimes you have to begin even when you have no chance of winning. Write down something where starting matters more than the outcome.
js_174: When rules and conscience clash, which side would I stand on?
js_175: The sheriff in the final chapter chose a person over the law. Think about where your own lines are — which ones you’d hold, and which you’d cross.
